title: The goddess and the flowers
hookLine: flowers fall on everyone; they slide off the bodhisattvas but stick to the disciples who think flowers improper

lines: A GODDESS WHO LIVES IN THE HOUSE.
cards: Petals begin to drift down from nowhere, over the whole crowded room. Someone in Vimalakirti's house has been listening all along: a goddess who lives there.

She's so delighted by what she's heard that she shows herself and scatters heavenly flowers over everyone, bodhisattvas and disciples alike. It should be a lovely moment. For some of the guests, it is.
For others, it turns into a small, very public struggle with a flower.

teach.b: Here's what happens, paraphrased. The flowers touch the bodhisattvas and fall away.
On the great disciples, they stick. Shariputra tries to brush them off his robe. They stay.
The others try, even using their powers. They stay. So the goddess asks him, mildly: why are you trying to get rid of them?
Flowers aren't proper for a monk, Shariputra says. He means the monastic rule against adornment; a monk doesn't wear garlands. The goddess answers: don't call the flowers improper.
The flowers don't think about proper and improper.
You're the one making that distinction, and for someone who has left home for the teaching, clinging to distinctions like that is what's out of place.
The flowers don't stick to the bodhisattvas, because they've let go of those distinctions. Then a picture.

When someone is afraid, harmful spirits find an opening; when fear is gone, nothing can get a grip. In the same way, the things of the senses cling to those who are afraid of them, and slide off those who aren't.

Some readers hear a hard question about rules here. The goddess isn't telling monks to throw out their precepts. Her target is the gripping: holding a rule so tightly that a gift from the sky becomes a stain.
It's the week's last day, so look back. The Lotus entrusted. A library of sutras opened.
A sick layman, disciples who all declined, a room that grew, a sickness born of compassion, and now flowers that stick only where someone is pushing them away.

how: Teachers in Mahayana traditions use the goddess and the flowers to talk about attachment to distinctions, while monastic communities in these traditions continue to keep their precepts.

games.q: what does “the goddess and the flowers” mean?
o: an offering of petals left at a goddess's shrine
flowers the Buddha gives to monks who keep every rule
flowers that cling only to those who push them away

games.q: the goddess and the flowers: tap the pairs.
p: the flowers fall away from them
flowers aren't proper for a monk

s: the flowers stuck to everyone in the room
they fell away from the bodhisattvas and stuck only to the disciples.
Shariputra couldn't shake them off, even with his powers
the disciples tried every way, and the flowers stayed.
the goddess tells the monks to give up their precepts
her point is about clinging to distinctions, not about throwing out rules.

games.q: you're Shariputra. heavenly flowers have landed on your robe, and a monk doesn't wear garlands. what do you do?
o: try every way to brush them off.
gather them up as an offering.
games.why: he tries to brush them off, and so do the others, even with their powers. the flowers stay, and the goddess asks why.

practice: Bring to mind one of your own small rules, not a deep moral line: how the dishwasher gets loaded, where the shoes go. Notice how tightly you hold it, and the little flare when someone breaks it.
On an out-breath, loosen the grip slightly, like opening a fist; the rule can stay, only the grip changes.

wordCard.voice: The goddess and the flowers. Heavenly flowers slide off the bodhisattvas and stick to the disciples who call them improper. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a deity, a goddess or god; the sutra's goddess who lives in Vimalakirti's house.

carryVoice: Your line: the flowers stick. Not to the robe, but to the grip. That was the week.
